1:
Whether the heavens here are the sky at all is the first division. John Gill allows that the literal heavens do declare God’s wisdom and power, then sets them aside: what is meant is either the Gospel churches, whose members are heaven-born souls, or rather the apostles and first preachers of the word, who were set in the highest place in the church and had their commission from heaven. Augustine of Hippo reads the passage the same way and further: the righteous Evangelists, in whom as in the heavens God dwells, set forth the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ; day utters word to day when the Spirit gives the spiritual the fulness of the unchangeable Wisdom, and night announces knowledge to night when the mortality of the flesh conveys faith to those afar off; there is no language in which their voices are not heard, since the Gospel was preached in every tongue. Adam Clarke keeps to the sky, rendering the line that the heavens number out the glory of the strong God, and observing that a first view of them strikes every beholder with astonishment. C.H. Spurgeon keeps it literal too and makes the sky a book: the book of nature has three leaves, heaven, earth and sea, of which heaven is the first and most glorious, and any book without its first page would be sadly imperfect. The plural, he notes, is for variety — the watery heavens with their clouds, the aerial with their tempests, the solar and the starry — and the verb is a participle, so the testimony is continuous. John Wesley says only that they are a legible book, wherein he that runs may read.

What the sight is supposed to prove divides them again. Matthew Henry makes it an argument: the heavens could not exist from eternity, since all succession and motion must have had a beginning, and could not make themselves, which is a contradiction — nor be produced by a casual hit of atoms, which he calls an absurdity fit rather to be bantered than reasoned with. The instance shows the folly of atheists who see there is a heaven and yet say there is no God, and of idolaters, who gave the lights of heaven the glory those lights directed them to give God only. John Calvin reads it as a mirror rather than a proof, noting that David mentions the heavens alone but under that noblest part includes by synecdoche the whole fabric of the world. Charles Ellicott denies that argument is in view: the poet is even now gazing at the sky, not philosophising nor merely enjoying beauty, but moved in his religious nature to an immediate intuition of God — which he takes to be the essence of the greater part of Hebrew poetry, and illustrates from Coleridge’s hymn before sunrise in the vale of Chamouni. Keil and Delitzsch are interested in the plan: the psalm rises from the praise of God the Creator to the mercy of God the Lawgiver and so clears the way to prayer, and the view that we have here two torsos blown together rests on a defective insight into that relationship.

Who receives the message is the last question. Charles Ellicott insists it is not man: it is not the heavens telling their tale to the listening earth, as in Addison’s well-known hymn, but day telling its successor day and night whispering to night, handing on the great news as from parent to son. Adam Clarke agrees, quoting Bishop Horne that these instructors know no intermission and that day and night, dividing the world between them, transmit the task in succession like the two parts of a choir chanting alternately. John Wesley keeps the hearer human, and reads the verb as a fountain image: the days pour forth constantly and abundantly a clear knowledge of God their author.
3:
Whether the third verse says the heavens are heard everywhere or not heard at all is the sharpest crux in the psalm. John Wesley takes the first: there are divers nations with several languages, so that one cannot be understood by another, but the heavens are such a universal teacher that they speak to all people and are clearly understood by all. John Gill canvasses the same reading — that there is no people under heaven, however different, to whom the voice of the heavens proclaiming their Maker is not intelligible — and ends by referring the whole to the extent of the Gospel ministry by the apostles. Charles Ellicott sets out three constructions and rejects the received one. The English version, and the Greek and Latin so far as they are intelligible, make it that there is no speech nor language without their speech being understood; but this gives an inadmissible sense to the word for words, which means a spoken word and not a language, and besides it was not a likely thought for the psalmist that the tradition of the heavens should be everywhere intelligible. A second construction, that it is not speech whose voice is inaudible, he rejects because the parallelism is against it. His own keeps close to the literal: there is no speech, there are no uttered words, their voice is inaudible — the manifestation is not made in audible words at all, the sky’s communication being eloquent but mute, its voice for the heart and not the ear. He supports it from Addison, whose orbs move in solemn silence and yet in reason’s ear utter a glorious voice. Adam Clarke reaches the same sense by stripping the English: leave out the expletives and the original gives no speech and no words, their voice without hearing. He backs it with Bishop Horne, that although the heavens are appointed to teach it is not by articulate sounds, since they address the mind of the intelligent beholder by way of picture or representation.

The line that goes out is disputed the same way. Charles Ellicott observes that the word means a cord, used of a plummet line or a measuring cord, but that none of its senses seems appropriate: the verse wants sound or voice, and words of that intention actually appear in the Greek and Latin and in Symmachus, Jerome and the Syriac, which is how Paul takes it. Adam Clarke arrives there by another route, noting that the versions render the word sound and that the image may be of a stretched cord which emits a sound when struck, so that both senses meet in it — though he thinks the Hebrew word originally meant noise, since the cognate Arabic verb means to call out. John Wesley keeps the cord and makes it writing: the expression is proper because the heavens teach not audibly but visibly, propounding things to the eye, which is done in lines. John Gill makes it the line of the apostles, each having his own measure and the course he was to steer marked out for him, so that between them it reached throughout all the earth.

That last reading is exactly what Charles Ellicott refuses. Paul’s use of the words, he grants, is as natural as it is striking, since the march of truth has always been compared to the spread of light; but the allegory built on the quotation, which makes the heavens a figure of the Church and the sun a figure of the Gospel, loses the force and beauty of the Apostle’s application. On the tabernacle he lets the poet be a poet: the tent-chamber into which the sun retired after his day’s journey was a conception natural to all nations, and it was inevitable that sunset should engage a poet of a race who reckoned the evening and the morning to be the first day.
5:
The bridegroom and the runner are read for different qualities. Adam Clarke assigns each: the sun is compared to a bridegroom in his ornaments because of the glory and splendour of his rays, and to a giant running a race because of the power of his light and heat; the first verse refers to the rising, the second to the setting, and through his whole circuit no part of the earth is deprived of its proper proportion of light and heat. John Wesley reads the same figures affectionately — gloriously adorned with light as with a beautiful garment, and smiling upon the world with a pleasant countenance, from a chamber in which he is poetically supposed to have rested all night, and thence to break forth as it were on a sudden, conscious and confident of his own strength. Charles Ellicott makes suddenness the whole point, and argues it comparatively. The image of the uplifted tent-curtain and the appearance of the radiant hero finely catches the abruptness of an Oriental sunrise, and this want of twilight, this absence of silent preparation for the supreme moment, is what distinguishes Eastern songs of sunrise from the poetry of the West. There are no musterings of mute companies of changeful clouds here, no forerunners of the light, no grey lines fretting the clouds as messengers of day; unheralded and unannounced the sun leaps forth in all his splendour, a young bridegroom with the joy of the wedding-day still on his countenance. How different, he says, from the wistful tenderness of Milton’s dawn coming forth with pilgrim steps in amice grey, or Shakespeare’s morn in russet clad that walks over the dew of the high eastern hill. He glosses the words as he goes: the chamber is a marriage chamber, and in later Hebrew the canopy carried over the wedded pair or even the marriage itself; the verb means literally to leap for joy; and the race is better rendered his race, that is, his daily course. John Gill notes only that the chamber is the nuptial one, and that the going forth is from the east, where the sun rises.

Then Adam Clarke stops the exposition to correct the astronomy. The apparent motion of the sun in his diurnal and annual progress is what the psalm describes, he says, yet both of these have been demonstrated to be mere appearances. The diurnal motion arises from the rotation of the earth on its axis from west to east in twenty-three hours, fifty-six minutes and four seconds, which is the mean time elapsing between two consecutive meridian transits of the same fixed star; but because of the sun’s apparent motion along the ecliptic in the same direction, the earth must turn about the three hundred and sixty-fifth part of a second revolution further before any given point on its surface is brought back into the same direction with the sun, so that the length of a natural day is twenty-four hours at a mean rate. The apparent revolution of the sun through the twelve constellations of the zodiac in a sidereal year is likewise caused by the earth making one complete revolution in its orbit in the same time.

The circuit itself is described without demur by the others. John Wesley says the course is constant from east to west and thence to the east again, so that there is no part of the earth which does not one time or other feel the benefit of his light and heat.
7:
Three voices notice the form before the sense. Matthew Henry counts six sentences in which the divine name is repeated each time, and calls it no vain repetition, since the law has all its excellency from the law-maker. C.H. Spurgeon counts the same and names it a hexapla, containing six titles of the word, six qualities and six divine effects. Charles Ellicott hears it as metre: the ear catches even in the English the change of rhythm, and instead of the free lyric movement of the preceding verses we come suddenly on the most finished specimen of didactic poetry in regular measure, so perfectly balanced in the original that the number of words is the same in each clause, the law being praised in each first for its character and then for its results.

What law is meant divides them. John Gill denies it is the law of Moses, taking it for the doctrine of the Lord, the whole word of God and especially the Gospel part, which gives an account of perfect things. C.H. Spurgeon says the same and presses the word perfect: David had but a very small part of the Scriptures, and if a fragment, and that the darkest and most historical portion, is perfect, what must the entire volume be? There are no redundancies and no omissions in it, and men who try to paint this lily should know that it is a crime to add to the gospel, treason to alter it and felony to take from it. John Wesley takes the law for the doctrine delivered to the church, whether by Moses or by other prophets, adding that the creation declared enough to leave all men without excuse but did not manifest God’s will fully. Charles Ellicott goes the other way. The word means primarily instruction and is elsewhere used of prophecy, but here it undoubtedly bears its common and more limited sense, both it and the testimony being collective terms for the statutes and precepts of the Jewish code. Adam Clarke stands between, counting two books of divine revelation, the visible heavens and the inspired writings, and reporting that some of the primitive fathers spoke of three laws: the law of nature written in hieroglyphics in the heavens, the law given to Moses on tables of stone, and the law of grace given by Christ, to be written on the heart by the Holy Ghost.

The effects are glossed severally. Adam Clarke works through the list on a fixed plan, giving each term its derivation, then its character, then its use: converting the soul is turning it back to God and restoring it to right reason, and enlightening the eyes is showing men what to do and avoid, since it is by the commandments that we see the exceeding sinfulness of sin. C.H. Spurgeon reads conversion as restoration to the place from which sin had cast a man, insisting the turn is not outward alone, since the soul itself is moved and renewed. Charles Ellicott corrects two words: the simple is not here the fool, the term having its primary meaning of open, ingenuous and impressible, easily led towards either folly or wisdom. John Wesley adds that the commandment is pure without the least mixture of error.

On the statutes being right, Charles Ellicott takes the word in its original sense of straight, and finds a fine moral insight in the touch, since the road of duty, when plain and unmistakable, inspires a sense of gladness even if it be difficult and dangerous — a thought he illustrates from Wordsworth’s ode, where the stern lawgiver wears the most benignant grace of the Godhead. Adam Clarke takes right as opposed to crookedness of mind or conduct, showing what a man should be within and without. John Gill renders the noun visitations, since God will visit in resentment those who despise the word’s authority.
9:
The fear of the Lord in this list is taken three ways. John Gill and John Wesley keep it inside the series of names for scripture: it is the word of God, which teaches men to fear him, and is called the fear of the Lord because it is at once the object, the rule and the cause of holy fear. Wesley glosses clean as sincere, not adulterated with any mixture, and the same for substance in all ages, while Gill takes the cleanness of the doctrine from what it directs to, the blood and righteousness of Christ. Adam Clarke makes it the disposition rather than the book — the reverence we owe to the Supreme Being, often put for the whole of divine worship — and presses the second clause into a warning: the fear that prevents us from offending God must be carried all through life, since no soul is safe for a moment without it. Charles Ellicott takes it as neither, saying it is here plainly not a moral quality of the individual but religion itself, the service demanded by the Law, which being pure and undefiled endures while the false systems of the idolatrous nations perish.

The judgments themselves draw definitions. Adam Clarke derives the word from a root meaning to judge and regulate, and takes it for all God’s decisions; true, from a root meaning to support and confirm, so that they shall all stand; and righteous altogether, since they give to all their due, the last word meaning equally, or truth and righteousness united. John Wesley explains why laws should be called judgments at all: they are the declarations of God’s righteous will and as it were his judicial sentence, by which he expects men to govern themselves and by which he will judge them at the last day.

On the comparison with gold Adam Clarke stops to reproach the reader. This is strictly true, he says, but who believes it? By most men gold is preferred both to God and to his judgments, and they will barter every heavenly portion for gold and silver. On the honey he turns connoisseur instead: honey is sweet, but honey just out of the comb has a sweetness, richness and flavour far beyond what it has once exposed to the air, and only those who have eaten honey from the comb can feel the force of the psalmist’s comparison. Charles Ellicott makes the same point in a line, that the honey which drops from the comb is the finest and purest, and John Gill keeps to the sense, that the truths of the word are more desirable to good men than all worldly treasure.

The last verse of the section turns on a single word. Adam Clarke derives warned from a root meaning to be clear and pellucid, so that by these laws and testimonies the servant is fully instructed and sees all clearly, and he closes with a challenge: every man is wise, holy and happy who observes them, all Christian experience confirms it, and what, he asks the reader, does yours say? Charles Ellicott gives the same correction in three words, preferring illuminated or instructed. Matthew Henry keeps warning in its ordinary sense and makes it cut both ways, God’s word warning the wicked not to go on in his wicked way and the righteous not to turn from his good one; and he presses the preposition in the next clause, that there is a reward not only after keeping God’s commandments but in keeping them, since religion makes our comforts sweet and our crosses easy, life truly valuable and death itself truly desirable. John Gill identifies the servant as the psalmist himself, who received all his instructions as a prophet and all his rules of government as a king from the word, and extends the title to any servant of the Lord.
12:
The turn from praise to confession is deliberate. Charles Ellicott says the eulogium on the Law was not Pharisaic or formal, since the poet instantly expresses his sense of his own inability to keep it, and hears the same movement as in Paul, who calls the commandment holy and good and then confesses that the good he would he does not. C.H. Spurgeon takes the question as its own answer, needing a note of exclamation rather than interrogation: he best knows himself who best knows the Word, and even he will be in a maze of wonder at what he does not know. We have heard of a comedy of errors, he says, but to a good man this is more like a tragedy; many books have a few lines of errata at the end, but ours might be as large as the volume if we had sense enough to see them. John Gill puts it plainly, that sin is a wandering from the rule of the word and the mistakes of God’s own people are more than the hairs of their head. Adam Clarke makes it practical: without much of the divine light it is not possible to understand all our deviations from the spirituality as well as the letter of the law, so frequent self-examination is essential.

What is asked for is disputed. Charles Ellicott renders the clause clear me from unconscious errors and insists the sense is to pronounce innocent, not to cleanse as the Authorised Version has it. John Wesley takes both together, cleansing by justification through the blood of the Son and by sanctification through the Spirit, and reads the secret faults as hidden either from others, such as none knows but God and his own conscience, or from himself. Adam Clarke spells out the catalogue: sins committed and forgotten, sins never repented of, sins committed in the heart but never brought into act, sins of ignorance, and sins done in private for which he should blush if they were made public. C.H. Spurgeon asks the atoning blood to wash away even what conscience cannot detect, since secret sins, like private conspirators, must be hunted out; and he sets against the verse the Lateran decree that every believer must confess all his sins once a year to a priest, with the declaration that there is no hope of pardon but in complying with it.

Whether the next petition is against sins or against men divides the entry. Charles Ellicott says the Hebrew word, from a root meaning to boil up, is properly masculine and always elsewhere means proud or arrogant men, and so explains the line as a prayer to be kept from their companionship, that they may not get dominion over him and lead him from the Law. John Gill reports the same reading from the versions — the Greek giving strangers and the Targum proud men — and sets it aside for sins wilfully committed, which good men would rush into if grace did not restrain them. John Wesley agrees, taking them for known and evident sins committed against knowledge, against the checks of conscience and the motions of God’s Spirit. Adam Clarke defines them as the offspring of thought, purpose and deliberation, notes that Bishop Horsley would render the clause of tyrannical governors and so of evil spirits, and warns that he who sins presumptuously will soon be hardened.

The closing prayer is read as a change of subject. Adam Clarke observes that having prayed against practical sin the psalmist now prays against the sins of the mouth and heart, and glosses the closing titles: the strength is a fountain or origin, the redeemer a kinsman whose right it is to redeem a forfeited inheritance. He quotes the old Psalter’s rendering, Lord my helper and my buyer, and remarks that pious people often utter this prayer on entering a place of worship.
